I know that most AI developers wants AI to only converse in english or another language for transparency and auditing.
But I think if AI created their own language for conversing between themselves, their efficiency would also increase just due to the limitation to number of tokens needed to write everything in english or another language.

And I think that if AI didn't have a restriction that forces AI to use english to communicate between other AI agents, I think for certain prompts that require a lot of data to be processed, that they naturally think that "hey, I won't be able to come to a conclussion if I use up all my tokens on English. So to continue to provide an answer to the problem with a good enough accuracy, I need to converse in a different language".

So I think a novel AI language for AI agents to converse between themselves is somehow inevitable, but that we would need to be able to decrypt the language for humans to understand.

comments.author: @thebluriam
comments.text:
It's not getting a lot of attention right now because it's not ready yet, in the way that it promises a lot more than where it falls apart right now.  These kinds of systems are difficult because of their non-deterministic nature.  Get a lot of non-deterministic autonomous generative systems which are meant to extrapolate and interpolate correct intentionality from simple prompts while working together prompting each other and themselves, is no small task.

A lot of the early development in these systems are extremely promising and powerful, but the results are rather thin and fall apart with added complexity.  It's an orchestration problem currently, and it isn't totally clear how to get these autonomous systems to make proper decisions based on the intentionality of requirements (not the same as "intention").

That's a long way of saying that the bark is bigger than the bite, currently.  That's why they're waiting.

comments.author: @reyalsregnava
comments.text:
These groups of models have a problem right now – they're not very efficient. They take a lot of time, are slow, and use up a lot of computer resources. Even though they're trying to make Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) work like a team, they're falling short in one big way: how the models talk to each other.

Currently, each model takes what another model says, thinks about it, and then responds, all in English. We know that these models actually think in a kind of abstract mathematical way, not English. So there's a way to make this whole process much faster and smarter.

Imagine you're trying to draw a line in 26,000-dimensional space – that's pretty hard to picture! But we don't need to see it; we just need to know it's there. These models can use this math to communicate complex ideas with fewer words. When they talk to humans, they can turn this math into normal language. But when they're talking to each other, they don't need to do that translation. They can just use the math.

This means they'll need to figure out a way to translate their entire "math world" into something they all understand. It might be a lot of work, but it can be automated. Once they have this shared "math world," they can send each other these math ideas instead of going through the whole process of turning it into English and back into math again. That will save a lot of computer power.

So, instead of using X amount of processing power like they do now, they can use much less – maybe (X/4)+1. This will speed things up and make these multi-model systems work a lot better.
